content: Broccoli is a plant that belongs to the cabbage family, scientifically known as Brassicaceae (formerly Cruciferae). It is classified under the Italica Cultivar Group of the species Brassica oleracea. Broccoli is characterized by its large, fleshy flower heads, which are typically green and arranged in a tree-like structure on branches that grow from a thick, edible stalk. These flower heads are surrounded by leaves. Broccoli closely resembles cauliflower, another cultivar group of the same species, but differs in its green color as opposed to cauliflower's white. In the United States, the term broccoli generally refers to the variety with a single large head, which is sometimes called Calabrese in the United Kingdom. In the UK, sprouting types (non-heading varieties) and those with underdeveloped flower buds are also sold as broccoli. The word broccoli originates from the Latin term broccolo, which is a diminutive form of the word for sprout. Broccoli is a cultivated form of wild cabbage, which remains the same species. Wild cabbage is believed to have originated along the northern and western coasts of the Mediterranean, where it was domesticated thousands of years ago. Over time, this domesticated cabbage was selectively bred into various forms, including broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, kale, kohlrabi, and Brussels sprouts, all of which belong to the same species. Historical references to broccoli are somewhat ambiguous. The Roman natural historian Pliny the Elder described a vegetable that fits the description of broccoli, suggesting that the Romans cultivated and consumed it during the 1st century. Some scholars also identify broccoli in the ancient Roman cookbook attributed to Apicius. Broccoli was primarily an Italian vegetable, as its name implies, long before it was introduced elsewhere. At that time, it was a sprouting type rather than the single large-headed variety seen today. Broccoli was first mentioned in France in 1560. However, as late as 1724, it was still unfamiliar in England, where Philip Miller's Gardener's Dictionary referred to it as a stranger and described it as sprout cauliflower or Italian asparagus. In the American colonies, Thomas Jefferson, an experimental gardener, planted broccoli at Monticello in 1767 alongside radishes, lettuce, and cauliflower. Despite this, broccoli remained an exotic vegetable in American gardens. In 1775, John Randolph of Virginia described broccoli as having stems that could be eaten like asparagus and heads that resembled cauliflower. Italian immigrants introduced broccoli to North America by 1806, but it did not gain widespread popularity until the 1920s. Commercial cultivation of broccoli in the United States began with the D’Arrigo brothers, Stefano and Andrea, Italian immigrants from Messina. They made initial plantings in San Jose, California, in 1922. A few crates of broccoli were shipped to Boston, where the Italian immigrant community in the North End embraced it. The broccoli business flourished, with the D’Arrigo brothers marketing their product under the brand name Andy Boy, named after Stefano’s young son Andrew, and promoting it through radio advertisements. There are three commonly grown types of broccoli. The most familiar type, often called Calabrese in Great Britain and simply broccoli in North America, has large green heads (10–20 cm in diameter) and thick stalks. It is named after Calabria, Italy, where it was first cultivated. This variety is an annual crop that thrives in cool seasons. Sprouting broccoli produces numerous smaller heads with thin stalks and is typically planted in May for harvest during winter or early the following year in temperate climates. Romanesco broccoli is notable for its distinctive fractal-like appearance and yellow-green color. It technically belongs to the Botrytis (cauliflower) cultivar group. Purple cauliflower, a type of broccoli sold in southern Italy, Spain, and the UK, has a cauliflower-like head composed of tiny flower buds, sometimes with a purple tint at the tips. Broccoli is a cool-weather crop that does not perform well in hot summer conditions. Other cultivar groups of Brassica oleracea include cabbage (Capitata Group), cauliflower (Botrytis Group), kale and collard greens (Acephala Group), kohlrabi (Gongylodes Group), and Brussels sprouts (Gemmifera Group). Chinese broccoli (Alboglabra Group) is also a cultivar group of Brassica oleracea. Broccoli is typically boiled or steamed but can also be eaten raw. It has become popular as a raw vegetable in hors d'oeuvre trays. Nutritionally, broccoli is rich in vitamin C and soluble fiber. It contains several bioactive compounds with potential anti-cancer properties, including diindolylmethane and selenium. The compound 3,3'-Diindolylmethane in broccoli is a potent modulator of the innate immune response system, exhibiting antiviral, antibacterial, and anti-cancer activities. Broccoli also contains glucoraphanin, which can be converted into the anti-cancer compound sulforaphane. However, boiling broccoli reduces its health benefits. High broccoli consumption has been associated with a reduced risk of aggressive prostate cancer. Broccoli leaves are also edible and contain significantly more beta-carotene than the florets. In popular culture, broccoli gained attention in 1928 when a cartoon in The New Yorker depicted a mother and child at the dinner table. The mother says, It's broccoli, dear, to which the child replies, I say it's spinach, and I say the hell with it. In politics, U.S. President George H. W. Bush famously expressed his dislike for broccoli during his presidency. In response, the broccoli agriculture lobby sent several tons of broccoli to the White House, which was subsequently donated to the Capital Area Food Bank. His son, President George W. Bush, mentioned in 2004 that he did not mind broccoli but preferred the florets over the stalks.
